arXiv:2501.18261v2 [hep-ph] 28 Aug 2025

A general upper bound on the light dark matter scattering rate in materials

Riccardo Catena Email: catena@chalmers.se    and Michał Iglicki Affiliation: Department of Physics, Chalmers University of Technology, SE-412 96 Göteborg, Sweden Email: michal.iglicki@chalmers.se
Abstract

Combining an effective theory description of spin-1/2 dark matter (DM)-electron interactions in materials with linear response theory provides a powerful framework to model the scattering of DM, including in-medium effects, in detectors used for direct searches. Within this framework, we show that the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions in detector materials admits a theoretical upper bound under general assumptions on the underlying DM-electron coupling. In particular, our theoretical upper bound applies to models where DM couples to the electron density as well as the spin, paramagnetic and Rashba currents in materials, and arises from the Kramers-Kronig relations that constrain the analytic properties of the scattering rate. We evaluate our maximum rate formula numerically for Ar, Xe, Ge, and Si targets and find that Ge and Si detectors are closer to saturate this theoretical upper bound, but still far from saturation when DM couples to densities or currents which are different from the electron density. This motivates the exploration of a different class of materials to effectively probe such coupling forms.

1 Introduction

The quest for dark matter (DM) is gradually broadening its focus, with a remarkable, global experimental effort directed towards probing models where the DM particle is approximately in the MeV to GeV mass range [1, 2, 3]. The experimental search for DM particles lighter than a GeV is motivated by the lack of discovery of WIMPs at direct detection experiments, and by the possibility of producing a DM candidate in this mass window with the correct cosmological abundance via the freeze-out mechanism (if the Lee-Weinberg bound [4] is circumvented by introducing the exchange of a new particle mediator in the relevant number-changing processes).

The search for DM-induced electronic transitions in germanium [5] and silicon [6, 7, 8], as well as liquid argon [9] and xenon [10], has so far played a major role in the exploration of the MeV to GeV mass window in direct detection experiments. The formalism for describing the scattering of Milky Way, sub-GeV DM particles on the electrons bound to a detector material has been put forward in [11, 12, 13], and subsequently extended to account for in-medium screening in models where DM couples to the electron density in the target [14, 15]. More recently, linear response theory has been used to further extend the formalism for DM-electron scattering in materials to effective theories where DM couples to all the electron densities and currents that arise at leading order in the non-relativistic expansion of the DM-electron scattering amplitude [16]. Effective theories for DM-electron interactions have been formulated in [17, 18], as well as in [19, 20].

Focusing on models where fermionic DM couples to the electron density, it has been pointed out that there exists a theoretical upper bound on the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions in a detector [21]. This bound arises from the so-called Kramers-Kronig relations, which follow from the analytic properties of the dielectric function, upon which the DM-induced electronic transition rate depends. This is an interesting observation, because it provides a systematic framework to identify optimal detector materials to probe the DM coupling to the electron density.

In this work, we show that a theoretical upper bound on the rate of spin-1/2 DM-induced electronic transitions exists not only in models where DM couples to the electron density, but also in models where it couples to the paramagnetic current, the spin current, the scalar product of spin and paramagnetic current, and the Rashba spin-orbit current. This extends the results of [21] to the leading currents and densities arising from the non-relativistic expansion of the DM-electron scattering amplitude, or, equivalently, from the non-relativistic expansion of the Dirac Hamiltonian [16]. Analogously to [21], the existence of the upper bound we find here follows from an application of the Kramers-Kronig relations. However, we do not apply the Kramers-Kronig relations to the dielectric function only, but also to the generalized susceptibilities that describe the linear response of materials to the leading, non-relativistic DM-electron couplings. For each given DM coupling, the ratio between the actual DM-induced electronic transition rate and our theoretical upper bound only depends on the assumed detector material and DM mass. For all currents and densities listed above, we evaluate this ratio focusing on Si, Ge, Ar, and Xe as detector materials. In general, we find that Si and Ge are closer to saturate our theoretical upper bound, but still far from saturation in all models where DM couples to densities or currents which are different from the electron number density. This points towards the need for a different class of materials to effectively probe such coupling forms.

Our work is organized as follows. In Sec. 2 we review the use of the Kramers-Kronig relations in the context of DM direct detection, and show why they imply a theoretical upper bound on the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions in models where DM couples to the electron density in the detector. In Sec. 3, we review the application of linear response theory to DM direct detection, and show that, for general DM-material couplings, the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions can be expressed in terms of generalized susceptibilities which, under general conditions, also obey the Kramers-Kronig relations. In Sec. 4.1, we use our generalized susceptibility formalism to obtain a theoretical upper bound on the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions in models where DM couples to the leading, non-relativistic electron densities and currents. In Sec. 4.2, we provide expressions for the interaction rate calculated in some specific effective models of DM-electron interactions. We evaluate our theoretical upper bound in Sec. 4.3, and conclude in Sec. 5. Additional results and useful identities, as well as a short discussion of some assumptions, are collected in the Appendices A, B, C and D.

2 Electronic transitions induced by a DM-electron density coupling

As already mentioned in the introduction, throughout the whole paper we assume the electrons to be non-relativistic, so that their kinetic energies are much smaller than mem_{e}. Nevertheless, some electrons in the material, namely, those at the innermost atomic shells, may be predominantly relativistic, as their expected kinetic energies are comparable to mem_{e}. Those electrons, however, are tightly bounded to the nucleus and, therefore, difficult to excite. Therefore, they do not significantly contribute to the total excitation rate. The valence electrons, whose excitations would be the main source of the DM-induced signal, are not subject to any significant relativistic corrections [22], so the non-relativistic treatment is justified.

2.3 Kramers-Kronig relations

vq≡𝒗⋅𝒒q=ωq+q2​mχ,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} v_{q}&\equiv\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\frac{\boldsymbol{q}}{q}\\ &=\frac{\omega}{q}+\frac{q}{2\,m_{\chi}}\,,\end{aligned} (26)

εr​(𝒒,ω)≃εr​(q,ω).\displaystyle\varepsilon_{r}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)\simeq\varepsilon_{r}(q,\omega)\,. (27)

Equations 22 and 23 can now be combined to obtain a theoretical upper bound, Γopt\Gamma_{\rm opt}, on Γ\Gamma [21]:

3 Electronic transitions induced by general DM-electron couplings

3.1 Fermi’s golden rule

In general, DM can couple to electron densities and currents in materials that are different from the electron number density n0n_{0}. Specifically, the most general form for the transition potential Veffs​s′V^{ss^{\prime}}_{\rm eff} at leading order in the electron velocity and in the momentum transfer is given by [16]

Vs​s′eff(𝒓e,𝒒)=−14​me​mχ​V{Fn0s​s′​ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e​ 1e+FnAs​s′​i2​me​[∇←𝒓e⋅𝝈e​ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e−ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e​𝝈e⋅∇→𝒓e]+𝑭𝒋5s​s′⋅𝝈e​ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e+𝑭𝒋Ms​s′⋅i2​me​[∇←𝒓e​ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e−ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e​∇→𝒓e]​𝟙e+𝑭𝒋Es​s′⋅12​me[∇←𝒓e×𝝈eei​𝒒⋅𝒓e+ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e𝝈e×∇→𝒓e]},\displaystyle\begin{aligned} V^{ss^{\prime}}_{\rm eff}(\boldsymbol{r}_{e},\boldsymbol{q})=-\frac{1}{4m_{e}m_{\chi}V}\,\Big\{\mkern 20.0mu&F_{n_{0}}^{ss^{\prime}}e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\,\mathds{1}_{e}\\ +\,&F_{n_{A}}^{ss^{\prime}}\frac{i}{2m_{e}}\left[\overleftarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}-e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\cdot\overrightarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\right]\\ +\,&\boldsymbol{F}_{\boldsymbol{j}_{5}}^{ss^{\prime}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\\ +\,&\boldsymbol{F}_{\boldsymbol{j}_{M}}^{ss^{\prime}}\cdot\frac{i}{2m_{e}}\left[\overleftarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}-e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}\overrightarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\right]\mathds{1}_{e}\\ +\,&\boldsymbol{F}_{\boldsymbol{j}_{E}}^{ss^{\prime}}\cdot\frac{1}{2m_{e}}\left[\overleftarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\times\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}+e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\times\overrightarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\right]\Big\}\,,\end{aligned} (29)

where an arrow on the gradient operator indicates whether it acts on the initial (∇→𝒓e\overrightarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}) or final (∇←𝒓e\overleftarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}) electron wave function, while the pre-factors Fn0s​s′F_{n_{0}}^{ss^{\prime}}, FnAs​s′F_{n_{A}}^{ss^{\prime}}, 𝑭𝒋5s​s′\boldsymbol{F}_{\boldsymbol{j}_{5}}^{ss^{\prime}}, 𝑭𝒋Ms​s′\boldsymbol{F}_{\boldsymbol{j}_{M}}^{ss^{\prime}}, and 𝑭𝒋Es​s′\boldsymbol{F}_{\boldsymbol{j}_{E}}^{ss^{\prime}} are model dependent. These pre-factors are listed in Appendix C for the effective theory of DM-electron interactions of [17, 18] and in Secs. 4.2.1, 4.2.2 and 4.2.3 for specific models where DM has as an anapole, electric dipole, or magnetic dipole moment.

The first line in Eq. 29 corresponds to the already discussed case of models where DM couples to the electron number density in materials. The third and fourth lines describe a coupling between DM and the electron spin or paramagnetic current, respectively. The second line can be identified with the spin-paramagnetic current coupling, and the last line with the Rashba term arising at second order in the 1/c1/c expansion of the Dirac Hamiltonian [16].

Inserting Eq. 29 into Eq. 3, and then the latter into Fermi’s golden rule, Eq. 1, we obtain the following expression for the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions in materials,

Γ\displaystyle\Gamma =116​me2​mχ2​∑a​b∫d​𝒒(2​π)3​∫d​𝒗​f​(𝒗)​ℱa​b​(𝒒,𝒗)​Kb†​a​(𝒒,ω𝒗,𝒒),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{16m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}\,\sum_{ab}\int\frac{{\rm d}\boldsymbol{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int{\rm d}\boldsymbol{v}\,f(\boldsymbol{v})\,\mathcal{F}_{ab}(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})K_{b^{\dagger}a}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega_{\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{q}})\,, (30)

where

ℱa​b(𝒒,𝒗)=12∑s​s′Fas​s′(𝒒,𝒗)Fbss′∗(𝒒,𝒗),\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{ab}(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ss^{\prime}}F^{ss^{\prime}}_{a}(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})\,F_{b}^{ss^{\prime}*}(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})\,, (31)

and Kb†​a​(𝒒,ω)K_{b^{\dagger}a}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) is the correlation function,

Kb†​a​(𝒒,ω)=2​πV​∑i​fe−β​EiZ​⟨f|a~​(−𝒒)|i⟩​⟨i|b~†​(𝒒)|f⟩​δ​(Ef−Ei−ω),\displaystyle K_{b^{\dagger}a}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)=\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{if}\frac{e^{-\beta E_{i}}}{Z}\,\langle f|\widetilde{a}(-\boldsymbol{q})|i\rangle\,\langle i|\widetilde{b}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{q})|f\rangle\,\delta(E_{f}-E_{i}-\omega)\,, (32)

while aa and bb could be any of the densities, or components of currents, contributing to Eq. 29, namely

(n~0,n~A,j~51,j~52,j~53,j~M1,….j~E1,…),\displaystyle(\widetilde{n}_{0},\,\,\widetilde{n}_{A},\,\,\widetilde{j}_{5_{1}},\,\,\widetilde{j}_{5_{2}},\,\,\widetilde{j}_{5_{3}},\,\,\widetilde{j}_{M_{1}},\,\,\dots.\,\,\widetilde{j}_{E_{1}},\,\,\dots)\,, (33)

where

n~0​(𝒒)\displaystyle\widetilde{n}_{0}(\boldsymbol{q}) ≡e−i𝒒⋅𝒓e,\displaystyle\equiv e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\,, (34a)

𝒋~5​(𝒒)\displaystyle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{j}}_{5}(\boldsymbol{q}) ≡𝝈ee−i𝒒⋅𝒓e,\displaystyle\equiv\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\,e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\,, (34c)
𝒋~M​(𝒒)\displaystyle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{j}}_{M}(\boldsymbol{q}) ≡i2​me[∇←𝒓ee−i𝒒⋅𝒓e−e−i𝒒⋅𝒓e∇→𝒓e],\displaystyle\equiv\frac{i}{2m_{e}}\left[\overleftarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}-e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}\overrightarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\right]\,, (34d)
𝒋~E​(𝒒)\displaystyle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{j}}_{E}(\boldsymbol{q}) ≡12​me[∇←𝒓e×𝝈ee−i𝒒⋅𝒓e+e−i𝒒⋅𝒓e𝝈e×∇→𝒓e].\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2m_{e}}\left[\overleftarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\times\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\,e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}+e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\times\overrightarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\right]\,. (34e)

We denote by 𝝈e=(σ1,σ2,σ3)\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}=(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma_{3}) the three-dimensional vector whose components are the Pauli matrices. For increased readability, in the remaining part of this work, we omit the tildes (e.g., we write n0n_{0} instead of n~0\widetilde{n}_{0}). In other words, all the densities and currents are hereafter meant to be expressed in momentum space.

3.2 Generalized susceptibility formalism

As the density-density correlation function Kn0​n0K_{n_{0}n_{0}} in Eq. 17 is related to the dielectric function, so is the correlation function Kb†​aK_{b^{\dagger}a} related to generalized susceptibilities describing the linear response of materials to a perturbation induced by general DM-electron couplings [16].

Indeed, in the interaction picture, Veffs​s′V_{\rm eff}^{ss^{\prime}} can be written as a time dependent perturbation [16]:

Veffs​s′(t)=−∑a∫d𝒓Ba(𝒓)Sas​s′(𝒓,t),\displaystyle V_{\rm eff}^{ss^{\prime}}(t)=-\sum_{a}\int{\rm d}\boldsymbol{r}\,B_{a}(\boldsymbol{r})\,S_{a}^{ss^{\prime}}(\boldsymbol{r},t)\,, (35)

with

Ba​(𝒓)=∫d​𝒒′(2​π)3​ei​𝒒′⋅𝒓​a​(𝒒′),\displaystyle B_{a}(\boldsymbol{r})=\int\frac{{\rm d}\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\,a(\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime})\,, (36)

and

Sas​s′​(𝒓,t)=14​me​mχ​V​Fas​s′​ei​𝒒⋅𝒓​e−i​ω𝒗,𝒒​t.\displaystyle S_{a}^{ss^{\prime}}(\boldsymbol{r},t)=\frac{1}{4m_{e}m_{\chi}V}\,F_{a}^{ss^{\prime}}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\,e^{-i\omega_{\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{q}}t}\,. (37)

Notice that at t=0t=0 Eqs. 35 and 29 coincide. In linear response theory, the fluctuation, ⟨Δ​a​(𝒓,t)⟩\langle\Delta a(\boldsymbol{r},t)\rangle, induced on the generic electron density or component aa by the potential Veffs​s′​(t)V_{\rm eff}^{ss^{\prime}}(t) is given by

⟨Δ​a​(𝒓,t)⟩\displaystyle\langle\Delta a(\boldsymbol{r},t)\rangle =∑b∫−∞td​t′​∫d​𝒓′​χa​b​(𝒓−𝒓′,t−t′)​Sbs​s′​(𝒓′,t′),\displaystyle=\sum_{b}\int_{-\infty}^{t}{\rm d}t^{\prime}\int{\rm d}\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}\,\chi_{ab}(\boldsymbol{r}-\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime},t-t^{\prime})\,S_{b}^{ss^{\prime}}(\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\,, (38)

where

χa​b​(𝒓−𝒓′,t−t′)≡i​θ​(t−t′)​⟨[a⁡(𝒓,t),b⁡(𝒓′,t′)]⟩\displaystyle\chi_{ab}(\boldsymbol{r}-\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime},t-t^{\prime})\equiv i\theta(t-t^{\prime})\Big\langle\left[a(\boldsymbol{r},t),b(\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\right]\Big\rangle (39)

is the generalized susceptibility associated with aa and bb. The double Fourier transform of χa​b\chi_{ab} obeys [16]

χa​b​(𝒒,ω)−χb†​a†∗​(𝒒,ω)=i​Ka​b​(𝒒,ω)​(1−e−β​ω).\displaystyle\chi_{ab}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)-\chi^{*}_{b^{\dagger}a^{\dagger}}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)=iK_{ab}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)\left(1-e^{-\beta\omega}\right)\,. (40)

In the T→0T\rightarrow 0 limit (see a short discussion in Sec. D.2), when 1−e−β​ω→11-e^{-\beta\omega}\rightarrow 1, we can use Eq. 40 to rewrite the transition rate Γ\Gamma, given by Eq. 30, as

Γ\displaystyle\Gamma =−i16​me2​mχ2​∑a​b∫d​𝒒(2​π)3​∫d​𝒗​f​(𝒗)​ℱa​b​(𝒒,𝒗)​(χa†​b−χb†​a∗)​(𝒒,ω𝒗,𝒒),\displaystyle=\frac{-i}{16m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}\,\sum_{ab}\int\frac{{\rm d}\boldsymbol{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int{\rm d}\boldsymbol{v}\,f(\boldsymbol{v})\,\mathcal{F}_{ab}(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})\left(\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}-\chi^{*}_{b^{\dagger}a}\right)(\boldsymbol{q},\omega_{\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{q}})\,, (41)

with the DM velocity distribution function ff defined by Eq. 25 and ℱa​b\mathcal{F}_{ab} given by Eq. 31.

3.3 Kramers-Kronig relations

In the time domain, the generalized susceptibilities χa†​b​(𝒒,t−t′)\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},t-t^{\prime}) are causal, as one can see from their definition, Eq. 39. In particular, this implies χa†​b​(𝒒,t−t′)=0\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},t-t^{\prime})=0 for t−t′<0t-t^{\prime}<0. Consequently, in the (complex) frequency domain χa†​b​(𝒒,ω)\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) is analytic in the upper-half plane, that is, for Im​ω≥0{\rm Im}\,\omega\geq 0. Apart of that, χa†​b​(𝒒,ω)→0\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)\rightarrow 0 for |ω|→∞|\omega|\rightarrow\infty. Moreover, χa†​b​(𝒒,t−t′){\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},t-t^{\prime})} is real in the time domain, which implies that, as a function of ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R}, Re​χa†​b​(𝒒,ω){\rm Re}\,\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) is even while Im​χa†​b​(𝒒,ω){\rm Im}\,\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) is odd.

Since χa†​b​(𝒒,ω)\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) meets the above three conditions for every 𝒒\boldsymbol{q}, it also obeys [23]

Re​χa†​b​(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle{\rm Re}\,\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) =1π​𝒫​∫−∞+∞d​ω′ω′−ω​Im​χa†​b​(𝒒,ω′),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\pi}\mathcal{P}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{{\rm d}\omega^{\prime}}{\omega^{\prime}-\omega}\,{\rm Im}\,\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega^{\prime})\,, (42a)
Im​χa†​b​(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle{\rm Im}\,\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) =−1π𝒫∫−∞+∞d​ω′ω′−ωReχa†​b(𝒒,ω′),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\pi}\mathcal{P}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{{\rm d}\omega^{\prime}}{\omega^{\prime}-\omega}\,{\rm Re}\,\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega^{\prime})\,, (42b)

as well as

∫0+∞d​ωω​Im​χa†​b​(𝒒,ω)=π2​χa†​b​(𝒒,0).\displaystyle\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{{\rm d}\omega}{\omega}\,{\rm Im}\,\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)=\frac{\pi}{2}\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},0)\,. (43)

The identities in Eq. 42 are the Kramers-Kronig relations for the generalized susceptibilities χa†​b​(𝒒,ω)\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}(\boldsymbol{q},\omega), while Eq. 43 extends the relation in Eq. 22 to the case of general DM couplings.

4 Upper bound on the transition rate for general DM-electron couplings

In this section, we first analytically derive a general upper bound on the DM-induced electronic transition rate (Sec. 4.1) and provide expressions for the interaction rate in specific effective models of DM (Sec. 4.2). We then numerically evaluate the transition rate to associated upper bound ratio focusing on germanium, silicon, argon and xenon detectors, and on models where DM exhibits an anapole, magnetic dipole or electric dipole moment (Sec. 4.3). This numerical analysis will allow us to assess which material is closest to saturate our general upper bound on Γ\Gamma.

4.1 Derivation from the Kramers-Kronig relations

We start from an analytic derivation of a general upper bound on Γ\Gamma based on the generalized Kramers-Kronig relations that apply to material responses beyond the familiar dielectric function.

Using Eq. 43, we now show that the sum of Eq. 41 is bounded from above. Let us recall Eq. 41:

Γ\displaystyle\Gamma =−i16​me2​mχ2​∑a​b∫d​𝒒(2​π)3​∫d​𝒗​f​(𝒗)​ℱa​b​(𝒒,𝒗)​(χa†​b−χb†​a∗)​(𝒒,ω𝒗,𝒒).\displaystyle=\frac{-i}{16m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}\,\sum_{ab}\int\frac{{\rm d}\boldsymbol{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int{\rm d}\boldsymbol{v}\,f(\boldsymbol{v})\,\mathcal{F}_{ab}(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})\left(\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}-\chi^{*}_{b^{\dagger}a}\right)(\boldsymbol{q},\omega_{\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{q}})\,. (44)

We begin by performing the change of integration variables introduced in Appendix B to obtain

Note that, though formally the integration in Eq. 53 is performed over 0<q<∞0<q<\infty and 0<ω<∞0<\omega<\infty, its range is effectively limited by the DM velocity distribution ff to

0\displaystyle 0 <q<qmax,\displaystyle<q<q_{\max}\,, qmax\displaystyle q_{\max} ≡2​mχ​(v⊕+vesc),\displaystyle\equiv 2\,m_{\chi}\,(v_{\oplus}+v_{\text{esc}})\,, (55a)
0\displaystyle 0 <ω<ωmax​(q),\displaystyle<\omega<\omega_{\max}(q)\,, ωmax​(q)\displaystyle\omega_{\max}(q) ≡q⁡(v⊕+vesc)−q22​mχ,\displaystyle\equiv q\,(v_{\oplus}+v_{\text{esc}})-\frac{q^{2}}{2\,m_{\chi}}\,, (55b)

corresponding to vq<v<v⊕+vescv_{q}<v<v_{\oplus}+v_{\text{esc}}. Moreover, the energy transfer ω\omega is required to exceed the 1-electron ionization threshold, which subsequently imposes a threshold on the DM mass, as explained in results discussion in Sec. 4.3.

Inspection of the explicit form of the functions ℱa​b\mathcal{F}_{ab} given in Appendix C shows that in general one has

ℱi​(q,ω,v)=ℱi(0)​(q,ω)+v2​ℱi(2)​(q,ω),\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{i}(q,\omega,v)=\mathcal{F}_{i}^{(0)}(q,\omega)+v^{2}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{(2)}(q,\omega)\,, (56)

where we made explicit that ℱi​(q,ω,v)\mathcal{F}_{i}(q,\omega,v) is either independent of vv, or it depends on vv quadratically, cf. Eq. 111. For readability, let us now keep only the ℱi(0)\mathcal{F}_{i}^{(0)} term. Calculation for the other term, which will be restored at the very end, follows analogously.

The final result for Γ\Gamma must be real, and since all ℱi(0)\mathcal{F}^{(0)}_{i}’s are real in the considered models (as can be explicitly checked basing on Appendix C), the part of the integral containing the real part of (χi−χi′⁣∗)\left(\chi_{i}-\chi^{\prime*}_{i}\right) must vanish. We thus obtain

Γ\displaystyle\Gamma =132​π2​me2​mχ2​∑i∫0qmaxd​q​q2​∫0ωmax​(q)d​ω​ρ(0)​(ω,q)​ℱi(0)​(q,ω,v)​Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{32\pi^{2}m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}\,\sum_{i}\int_{0}^{q_{\max}}{\mathrm{d}}q\,q^{2}\int_{0}^{\omega_{\max}(q)}{\mathrm{d}}\omega\,\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,\mathcal{F}^{(0)}_{i}(q,\omega,v)\,\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega)\,, (57)

where

Δ​χi≡χi+χi′,\displaystyle\Delta\chi_{i}\equiv\chi_{i}+\chi^{\prime}_{i}\,, (58)

such that Im​Δ​χi=Im⁡(χi−χi′⁣∗)\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}=\mathrm{Im}\,(\chi_{i}-\chi^{\prime*}_{i}). Note that, in the definition of Δ​χi\Delta\chi_{i}, none of the susceptibilities is complex-conjugated, so that, similarly to each χa†​b\chi_{a^{\dagger}b}, every Δ​χi​(q,ω)\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega) (treated as a function of ω\omega) is analytic on the complex upper half-plane. Therefore, it also obeys the Kramers-Kronig relations.

To obtain the theoretical upper bound, we perform two consecutive estimations. Firstly, after dividing and multiply the integrand by 1=ω/ω1=\omega/\omega for further convenience, we replace the value of ω​ρ(0)​(ω,q)​ℱi(0)​(q,ω)\omega\,\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,\mathcal{F}^{(0)}_{i}(q,\omega) by its maximum for a given qq:

Γ≤132​π2​me2​mχ2∑i∫0qmaxdqq2maxω[ωρ(0)(ω,q)ℱ(0)i(q,ω)]××∫0ωmax​(q)d​ωω​Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \Gamma&\leq\frac{1}{32\pi^{2}m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}\,\sum_{i}\int_{0}^{q_{\max}}{\mathrm{d}}q\,q^{2}\,\max_{\omega}\left[\omega\,\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,\mathcal{F}^{(0)}_{i}(q,\omega)\right]\times\\ &\mkern 300.0mu\times\int_{0}^{\omega_{\max}(q)}\frac{{\mathrm{d}}\omega}{\omega}\,\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega)\,.\end{aligned} (59)

If, for a given value of ii, Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω)\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega) is non-negative for each ω\omega, the above estimation 59 is (for this particular ii) a trivial consequence of the fact that

ω​ρ(0)​(ω,q)​ℱi(0)​(q,ω)​Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω)≤maxω⁡[ω​ρ(0)​(ω,q)​ℱi(0)​(q,ω)]​Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω).\displaystyle\omega\,\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,\mathcal{F}^{(0)}_{i}(q,\omega)\,\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega)\leq\max_{\omega}\left[\omega\,\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,\mathcal{F}^{(0)}_{i}(q,\omega)\right]\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega)\,. (60)

This is not always the case; for instance, for q=15​ keVq=15\text{ keV} the value of the Im​Δ​χ𝒋M†​𝒋Mδ​(q,ω)\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi^{\delta}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{\dagger}_{M}\boldsymbol{j}_{M}}(q,\omega) coupling (relevant for the anapole model) calculated for Si is negative for each ω\omega. However, as we checked numerically, for each considered coupling and material, the integral over momenta is dominated by those values of qq for which Im​Δ​χi\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i} is predominantly positive, so that 59 is satisfied.

The second step makes use of the following inequality:

∫0ωmax​(q)d​ωω​Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω)≤π​U​(q)−1.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\omega_{\max}(q)}\frac{{\mathrm{d}}\omega}{\omega}\,\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega)\leq\pi\,U(q)^{-1}\,. (61)

To justify the above estimation for positive Im​Δ​χi\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}, we first extend the integration range:

∫0ωmax​(q)d​ωω​Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω)≤∫0∞d​ωω​Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω),\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\omega_{\max}(q)}\frac{{\mathrm{d}}\omega}{\omega}\,\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega)\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{{\mathrm{d}}\omega}{\omega}\,\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega)\,, (62)

and then, using the Kramers-Kronig relation 43, replace the integral on the right-hand side by the value at ω=0\omega=0:

∫0ωmax​(q)d​ωω​Im​Δ​χi​(q,ω)≤π2​Δ​χi​(q,0).\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\omega_{\max}(q)}\frac{{\mathrm{d}}\omega}{\omega}\,\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}(q,\omega)\leq\frac{\pi}{2}\,\Delta\chi_{i}(q,0)\,. (63)

Eventually, inequality 61 is obtained by using the estimation

Δ​χi​(q,0)≤2​U​(q)−1,\displaystyle\Delta\chi_{i}(q,0)\leq 2\,U(q)^{-1}\,, (64)

corresponding for χi=χn0​n0\chi_{i}=\chi_{n_{0}n_{0}} to εr−1>0\varepsilon_{r}^{-1}>0, which should be the case for most materials relevant for DM detection (see an extended discussion of this issue in [21]).

Neither condition 62 nor 64 is always satisfied; for example, 62 does not hold in the aforementioned case of Im​Δ​χ𝒋M†​𝒋Mδ​(q=15​ keV,ω)\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi^{\delta}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{\dagger}_{M}\boldsymbol{j}_{M}}(q=15\text{ keV},\omega) for Si, and 64 is broken by a factor of ca. 20 for the Δ​χ𝒋5†​𝒋5δ\Delta\chi^{\delta}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{\dagger}_{5}\boldsymbol{j}_{5}} coupling (relevant in the anapole and the magnetic dipole model) calculated for the same material at q=500​ eVq=500\text{ eV}. However, numerical tests confirm that, for all considered materials and couplings, inequality 61 is always fulfilled. The reason is that, for any coupling and material, at most one of inequalities 62 and 64 is broken at a time. If the first of them is fulfilled, the estimation 62 is very conservative for positive Im​Δ​χi\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i}’s, so that the final conclusion holds even though 64 is incorrect. Conversely, if Eq. 62 does not hold, it means that Im​Δ​χi\mathrm{Im}\Delta\chi_{i} is predominantly negative, so the integral in Eq. 61 can be limited from above by any positive value and one does not have to use 62 and the Kramers-Kronig relations to draw the final conclusion.

Using estimation 61 we obtain the following theoretical upper bound on the interaction rate:

Γ\displaystyle\Gamma ≤132​π​me2​mχ2​∑i∫0qmaxd​q​q2​maxω​[ω​ρ(0)​(ω,q)​ℱi(0)​(q,ω)]​U​(q)−1.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{32\pi m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}\,\sum_{i}\int_{0}^{q_{\max}}{\mathrm{d}}q\,q^{2}\,\max_{\omega}\left[\omega\,\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,\mathcal{F}^{(0)}_{i}(q,\omega)\right]U(q)^{-1}\,. (65)

In the general case of ℱi​(q,ω,v)=ℱi(0)​(q,ω)+v2​ℱi(2)​(q,ω)\mathcal{F}_{i}(q,\omega,v)=\mathcal{F}^{(0)}_{i}(q,\omega)+v^{2}\mathcal{F}^{(2)}_{i}(q,\omega) (cf. Eq. 56), we apply the same procedure and find:

Γ≤Γopt≡132​π​me2​mχ2∑i∫0qmaxdqq2maxω[ωρ(0)(ω,q)F(0)i(q,ω)+ωρ(2)(ω,q)F(2)i(q,ω)]U−1(q).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \Gamma&\leq\Gamma_{\text{opt}}\equiv\frac{1}{32\pi m_{e}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}\,\sum_{i}\int_{0}^{q_{\max}}{\mathrm{d}}q\,q^{2}\,\max_{\omega}\left[\omega\,\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,F^{(0)}_{i}(q,\omega)\right.\\ &\mkern 350.0mu+\left.\omega\,\rho^{(2)}(\omega,q)\,F^{(2)}_{i}(q,\omega)\right]U^{-1}(q)\,.\end{aligned} (66)

Equation 66 gives the theoretical upper bound on Γ\Gamma we find from the Kramers-Kronig relations. It is worth noting that due to the absence of χ\chi in the final result, this bound is independent of the choice of the detector material. Thus, a comparison of the actual interaction rate 57 with the result of Eq. 66 provides a way to evaluate the given material as a potential target in direct detection experiments. Below, we apply this general bound to the specific case of anapole, magnetic dipole, and electric dipole DM.

4.1.1 DM of spins different than 1/2

In our analysis, we assume the dark particles to have spin 1/2. Effective theory of interactions of DM of spin up to 11 with nucleons or electrons has been the topic of numerous works, including [24, 25, 26]. As can be observed from Table 1 of [26], to describe interactions between spin-1 DM and electrons one must employ more types of effective operators than in the fermion DM case. This would affect our calculations in two ways:

  1. 1.

    coefficients Fa​bF_{ab} for a,b=n0,nA,𝒋5,𝒋M,𝒋Ea,b=n_{0},n_{A},\boldsymbol{j}_{5},\boldsymbol{j}_{M},\boldsymbol{j}_{E}, given by Eqs. 115, 118 and 120, would contain more terms coming from the new operators depending on the generalized densities and currents analysed by us;

  2. 2.

    some of the effective operators relevant for spin-1 DM cannot be expressed in the form of our Eq. 29, so that including them would require indices aa and bb to cover a broader range of generalized densities and currents. For instance, operator 𝒪21\mathcal{O}_{21} defined in [26] requires introducing in Eq. 29 a term proportional to

    i2​me​[∇←𝒓e⋅𝓢Xsym⋅𝝈e​ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e−ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e​𝝈e⋅𝓢Xsym⋅∇→𝒓e],\displaystyle\frac{i}{2m_{e}}\,\left[\overleftarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}_{X}^{\text{sym}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}-e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}\cdot\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}_{X}^{\text{sym}}\cdot\overrightarrow{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\right]\;, (67)

    with (𝒮Xsym)i​j≡12​(SXi​SXj+SXj​SXi)(\mathcal{S}_{X}^{\text{sym}})^{ij}\equiv\frac{1}{2}(S_{X}^{i}S_{X}^{j}+S_{X}^{j}S_{X}^{i}), where 𝑺X\boldsymbol{S}_{X} denotes a vector formed by the spin operators of the vector DM particle. As can be observed, such a term cannot be decomposed into a DM-related and an e−e^{-}-related part in any other way than by introducing a generalized “electronic coupling tensor” 𝓙\boldsymbol{\mathcal{J}} given by

    𝒥i​j≡i2​me​[∂←𝒓ei​σej​ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e−ei​𝒒⋅𝒓e​∂→𝒓ej​σei].\displaystyle\mathcal{J}^{ij}\equiv\frac{i}{2m_{e}}\,\left[\overleftarrow{\partial}^{i}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\sigma_{e}^{j}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}-e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\,\overrightarrow{\partial}^{j}_{\boldsymbol{r}_{e}}\sigma_{e}^{i}\right]\;. (68)

Consequently, analysis of the vector DM case requires adding new contributions to the ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i} terms both in Eq. 57, which expresses the actual DM-e−e^{-} interaction rate, and in Eq. 66, which provides the theoretical upper bound. The ratio Γopt/Γ\Gamma_{\text{opt}}/\Gamma would depend on the new terms in a non-trivial way, so that it is difficult to predict to which extent our results would apply to the general vector DM case. Note that all the new contributions to the matrix element squared would be expressible in terms of the generalized susceptibilities employed in this work; no new generalized susceptibilities would be needed [26].

On the contrary, effective operators required to describe interactions of scalar DM with electrons form a subset of those employed in the fermion DM case. Therefore, adjusting our calculations to the spin-0 case would be straightforward, as it only requires dropping terms specific to the spin-1/2 case. However, precise values of the final ratio between the theoretical optimum and the actual interaction rate cannot be predicted prior to an actual calculation.

Regardless of the aforementioned differences in detailed forms of expressions and numerical results, the methodology we have used remains valid for any spin of DM particles, so that it can be straightforwardly extended and used to generalize our approach to the cases of DM of spins other than 1/2.

4.2 Interaction rate in specific effective models

4.2.1 Anapole

DM has an anapole moment if it couples to the photon via the higher order electromagnetic coupling,

ℒ=12​gΛ2​χ¯​γμ​γ5​χ​∂νFμ​ν,\displaystyle\mathscr{L}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{g}{\Lambda^{2}}\overline{\chi}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{5}\chi\,\partial^{\nu}F_{\mu\nu}\,, (69)

where Fμ​νF_{\mu\nu} is the electromagnetic field strength tensor, χ\chi is a Majorana four-component spinor describing the DM particle, gg is a coupling constant while Λ\Lambda is an energy scale. In the non-relativistic limit, Eq. 69 implies the following amplitude for DM scattering by a free electron [17],

ℳ=4​e​gΛ2​mχ​me​[2​(𝒗el⟂⋅ξ†s′​𝑺χ​ξs)​δr′​r+ge​(ξ†s′​𝑺χ​ξs)⋅(i​𝒒me×ξ†r′​𝑺e​ξr)],\displaystyle\mathscr{M}=\frac{4eg}{\Lambda^{2}}m_{\chi}m_{e}\left[2\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp}\cdot\xi^{\dagger s^{\prime}}\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\xi^{s}\right)\delta^{r^{\prime}r}+g_{e}\left(\xi^{\dagger s^{\prime}}\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\xi^{s}\right)\cdot\left(i\frac{\boldsymbol{q}}{m_{e}}\times\xi^{\dagger r^{\prime}}\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\xi^{r}\right)\right]\,, (70)

where 𝑺χ≡𝝈χ/2\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\equiv\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\chi}/2 (𝑺e≡𝝈e/2)(\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\equiv\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{e}/2) denotes the spin matrix corresponding to the dark particle (electron), ge=2g_{e}=2, and 𝒗el⟂\boldsymbol{v}_{\text{el}}^{\perp} is the so-called transverse relative velocity, which is the component of the relative DM-e−e^{-} velocity transverse to the momentum transfer in the case of elastic scattering. The associated transition potential depends on the electron density, paramagnetic current, and spin current [16]:

Vs​s′eff=−\displaystyle V^{ss^{\prime}}_{\rm eff}=- 14​me​mχ​V​[F0s​s′​n0​(−𝒒)+𝑭5s​s′⋅𝒋5​(−𝒒)+𝑭Ms​s′⋅𝒋M​(−𝒒)].\displaystyle\frac{1}{4m_{e}m_{\chi}V}\left[F_{0}^{ss^{\prime}}n_{0}(-\boldsymbol{q})+\boldsymbol{F}_{5}^{ss^{\prime}}\cdot\boldsymbol{j}_{5}(-\boldsymbol{q})+\boldsymbol{F}_{M}^{ss^{\prime}}\cdot\boldsymbol{j}_{M}(-\boldsymbol{q})\right]\,. (71)

where the functions F0s​s′F_{0}^{ss^{\prime}}, 𝑭5s​s′\boldsymbol{F}_{5}^{ss^{\prime}} and 𝑭Ms​s′\boldsymbol{F}_{M}^{ss^{\prime}} are listed in Eq. 115 with c8c_{8} and c9c_{9} explicitly given by

c8\displaystyle c_{8} =8​e​me​mχ​gΛ2,\displaystyle=8em_{e}m_{\chi}\frac{g}{\Lambda^{2}}\,, (72a)
c9\displaystyle c_{9} =−8​e​me​mχ​gΛ2,\displaystyle=-8em_{e}m_{\chi}\frac{g}{\Lambda^{2}}\,, (72b)

and all other coupling constants set to zero. By combining Eqs. 72, 118 and 57, we find

+ρ(2)(ω,q)ℱi(2)(q,ω)],\displaystyle\quad+\rho^{(2)}(\omega,q)\,\mathcal{F}^{(2)}_{i}(q,\omega)\Big]\,,

Figures 1, 2 and 3 show the ratio between the optimal total interaction rate Γopt\Gamma_{\text{opt}}, given by Eq. 66, and the actual total interaction rate Γ\Gamma, obtained for a given material from Eq. 57. The results presented in Fig. 1 have been obtained in the electric dipole model, described briefly in Sec. 4.2.3, while Figs. 2 and 3 correspond to the magnetic dipole (Sec. 4.2.2) and anapole (Sec. 4.2.1) models, respectively. In each plot, the thick green line represents the values obtained for silicon, the thin black line corresponds to germanium, the dotted blue line denotes the results for xenon and the dashed orange line has been obtained for argon. The horizontal red line marks the reference value of 11, for which the actual interaction rate Γ\Gamma would saturate the theoretical upper bound Γopt\Gamma_{\text{opt}}. Note that Γopt\Gamma_{\text{opt}} does not depend on the chosen material, so the plotted ratio can serve as an evaluation of a given material’s quality with respect to its usefulness in direct searches for DM.

The maximal energy transfer from a dark particle of mass mχm_{\chi}, which corresponds to a total absorption of its energy, is mχ​(v⊕+vesc)2/ 2m_{\chi}\,(v_{\oplus}+v_{\text{esc}})^{2}\,/\,2, where v⊕+vesc≈800​m/sv_{\oplus}+v_{\text{esc}}\approx 800~\text{m/s} is the maximal velocity of the dark particle according to the standard halo model (see Appendix A). For the materials considered in our manuscript, excitations caused by DM particles of masses lower than 0.1​MeV0.1~\text{MeV} would fail to exceed the 1-electron ionization threshold. In such a case, the detection method should be focused on different channels, such as phononic excitations. This can clearly be observed in our plots, where the ratio between the optimum and the actual rate tends to infinity as DM mass approaches the value corresponding to the 1-electron ionization threshold: mχ=0.19​MeVm_{\chi}=0.19~\text{MeV} for Ge, mχ=0.32​MeVm_{\chi}=0.32~\text{MeV} for Si, mχ=4.6​MeVm_{\chi}=4.6~\text{MeV} for Ar, mχ=3.6​MeVm_{\chi}=3.6~\text{MeV} for Xe.

It can be observed that, for Si and Ge detectors, the ratio approaches values around 10210^{2} in the electric dipole model, while in the anapole and the magnetic dipole model, the ratio is always very large, i.e., above 10410^{4}. This is correlated with the fact that the response to the density-density coupling (the only one relevant for the electric dipole) is close to the maximal possible, while the response to the Δ​χ𝒋M†​𝒋Mδ\Delta\chi^{\delta}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{\dagger}_{M}\boldsymbol{j}_{M}}, Δ​χ𝒋M†​𝒋Mq​q\Delta\chi^{qq}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{\dagger}_{M}\boldsymbol{j}_{M}} couplings which dominate for the anapole and the magnetic dipole, is far from optimal. In contrast, for Ar and Xe detectors, our theoretical upper bound is at least four orders of magnitude larger than the actual rate, regardless of the model. For all materials and models considered in this work, the ratio reported in Figures 1, 2 and 3 is minimal for a value of the DM particle mass in the range between 0.5 and 15 MeV.

5 Summary and conclusions

We investigated the analytic properties of the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions in materials within a framework that combines an effective theory description of DM-electron interactions with linear response theory. Within this framework, the rate of DM scattering events in materials can be expressed in terms of generalized susceptibilities describing the response of detectors to an external DM perturbation. We found that the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions in materials admits a theoretical upper bound under general assumptions on the underlying DM-electron coupling. This bound applies to models where DM couples to the electron density as well as the electron spin, paramagnetic and Rashba currents. We obtained this result by applying a set of the Kramers-Kronig relations to the generalized susceptibilities used in [16] to express the rate of DM-induced electronic transitions in materials.

We evaluated our theoretical upper bound numerically for Ar, Xe, Ge and Si targets and found that, while Ge and Si detectors are generically closer to saturate this theoretical upper bound, they are still far from saturation, unless DM couples to the electron density. This motivates the exploration of different classes of materials to effectively probe such coupling forms.

Let us work in a coordinate system where Earth’s velocity with respect to the galactic centre (denoted by 𝒗⊕\boldsymbol{v}_{\oplus}), DM velocity in the laboratory frame (𝒗\boldsymbol{v}), and momentum transfer (𝒒\boldsymbol{q}) are related by the following relations:

𝒗⊕\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}_{\oplus} =v⊕​𝒆z,\displaystyle=v_{\oplus}\,\boldsymbol{e}_{z}\,, (96a)
𝒗\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v} =v​R​(α,β)​𝒆z,\displaystyle=v\,R(\alpha,\beta)\,\boldsymbol{e}_{z}\,, (96b)
𝒒\displaystyle\boldsymbol{q} =q​R​(α,β)​R​(θ,ϕ)​𝒆z,\displaystyle=q\,R(\alpha,\beta)\,R(\theta,\phi)\,\boldsymbol{e}_{z}\,, (96c)

where

R⁡(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle R(\theta,\phi) ≡[cos⁡ϕ−sin⁡ϕ0sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ0001]​[cos⁡θ0sin⁡θ010−sin⁡θ0cos⁡θ]\displaystyle\equiv\left[\begin{array}[]{@{}ccc@{}}\cos\phi&-\sin\phi&0\\ \sin\phi&\cos\phi&0\\ 0&0&1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{@{}ccc@{}}\cos\theta&0&\sin\theta\\ 0&1&0\\ -\sin\theta&0&\cos\theta\end{array}\right]

is a rotation matrix, so that

𝒗⋅𝒗⊕\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_{\oplus} =v​v⊕​cos⁡α,\displaystyle=vv_{\oplus}\cos\alpha\,, 𝒗⋅𝒒\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{q} =v​q​cos⁡θ.\displaystyle=vq\cos\theta\,. (103)

Next, we perform the change of integration variables (𝒒,𝒗)→(q,ω,v,α,β,ϕ)(\boldsymbol{q},\,\boldsymbol{v})\rightarrow(q,\,\omega,\,v,\,\alpha,\,\beta,\,\phi), such that

d​𝒒​d​𝒗\displaystyle{\mathrm{d}}\boldsymbol{q}\,{\mathrm{d}}\boldsymbol{v} =q​d​q​d​ω​v​d​v​d​cos⁡α​d​β​d​ϕ,\displaystyle=q\,{\mathrm{d}}q\,{\mathrm{d}}\omega\,v\,{\mathrm{d}}v\,{\mathrm{d}}\cos\alpha\,{\mathrm{d}}\beta\,{\mathrm{d}}\phi\,, (104)

which, after integrating over the irrelevant angles β\beta and ϕ\phi (Γ\Gamma does not depend on them), turns to

d​𝒒​d​𝒗\displaystyle{\mathrm{d}}\boldsymbol{q}\,{\mathrm{d}}\boldsymbol{v} =4​π2​q​d​q​d​ω​v​d​v​d​cos⁡α.\displaystyle=4\pi^{2}\,q\,{\mathrm{d}}q\,{\mathrm{d}}\omega\,v\,{\mathrm{d}}v\,{\mathrm{d}}\cos\alpha. (105)

The integration range is

0\displaystyle 0 <q<∞,\displaystyle<q<\infty\,, 0\displaystyle 0 <ω<∞,\displaystyle<\omega<\infty\,, vq\displaystyle v_{q} <v<∞,\displaystyle<v<\infty\,, −1\displaystyle-1 <cos⁡α<1,\displaystyle<\cos\alpha<1\,, (106)

where

vq≡ωq+q2​mχ,\displaystyle v_{q}\equiv\frac{\omega}{q}+\frac{q}{2\,m_{\chi}}\,, (107)

and the ω>0\omega>0 requirement has been introduced for physical reasons. Note that the velocity vv is bounded from above by the cut-off value vesc+v⊕v_{\text{esc}}+v_{\oplus}, which is imposed via the step function in f⁡(𝒗)f(\boldsymbol{v}) (see Appendix A) and affects the actual range of integration over d​qdq and d​ωd\omega.

B.1 Velocity-independent BB

When the function BB introduced in Eq. 93 is independent of vv, the rate Γ\Gamma can be written as follows:

Γ=4​π​∫0∞q2​𝑑q​∫0∞d​ω​ρ(0)​(ω,q)​B​(ω,q),\displaystyle\Gamma=4\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}q^{2}{\mathrm{d}}q\int_{0}^{\infty}{\mathrm{d}}\omega\,\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,B(\omega,q)\,, (108)

where

ρ(0)​(ω,q)≡πq​∫vq∞v​𝑑v​∫−11d​cos⁡α​f​(𝒗).\displaystyle\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\equiv\frac{\pi}{q}\int_{v_{q}}^{\infty}v\,{\mathrm{d}}v\int_{-1}^{1}{\mathrm{d}}\cos\alpha\,f(\boldsymbol{v})\,. (109)

By analytically evaluating the angular and velocity integrals in the above equation, we find

ρ(0)​(ω,q)=𝒩​π​v022​q××{π2​v0v⊕​[erf(x+)+erf(x−)]−2​e−z2for ​vq<vesc−v⊕π2​v0v⊕​[erf(z)+erf(x−)]−(1+x−)​e−z2for ​vesc−v⊕<vq<vesc+v⊕0for ​vesc+v⊕<vq,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)&=\frac{\mathcal{N}\,\pi\,v_{0}^{2}}{2\,q}\,\times\\ &\mkern 10.0mu\times\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\,\frac{v_{0}}{v_{\oplus}}\left[\mathop{\mathrm{erf}}\left(x_{+}\right)+\mathop{\mathrm{erf}}\left(x_{-}\right)\right]-2\,e^{-z^{2}}&\text{for }v_{q}<v_{\text{esc}}-v_{\oplus}\\ \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\,\frac{v_{0}}{v_{\oplus}}\left[\mathop{\mathrm{erf}}\left(z\right)+\mathop{\mathrm{erf}}\left(x_{-}\right)\right]-\left(1+x_{-}\right)\,e^{-z^{2}}&\text{for }v_{\text{esc}}-v_{\oplus}<v_{q}<v_{\text{esc}}+v_{\oplus}\\ 0&\text{for }v_{\text{esc}}+v_{\oplus}<v_{q}\end{cases}\,,\mkern-60.0mu\end{aligned} (110)

where x+≡(v⊕+vq)/v0x_{+}\equiv(v_{\oplus}+v_{q})/v_{0}, x−≡(v⊕−vq)/v0x_{-}\equiv(v_{\oplus}-v_{q})/v_{0}, z≡vesc/v⊕z\equiv v_{\text{esc}}/v_{\oplus}, and the normalization constant 𝒩\mathcal{N} is provided in Appendix A.

B.2 Velocity-dependent BB

For the models studied in this work, the DM-electron scattering amplitude ℳ\mathscr{M} is at most linear in 𝒗\boldsymbol{v}. Consequently, the function BB can be at most quadratic in 𝒗\boldsymbol{v}:

B⁡(ω,q,v)=B(0)​(ω,q)+B(2)​(ω,q)​v2.\displaystyle B(\omega,q,v)=B^{(0)}(\omega,q)+B^{(2)}(\omega,q)\,v^{2}\,. (111)

The absence of terms linear in 𝒗\boldsymbol{v} follows from the fact that to contribute to a scalar function BB, they must be contracted with 𝒒\boldsymbol{q}. This product can be then expressed in terms of ω\omega and qq, see Eq. 95. The contribution to Γ\Gamma from B(0)B^{(0)} has been discussed in the previous subsection. In general,

Γ=∫d​𝒒​d𝒗​f​(𝒗)​B​(ω,q,v)=∫d​𝒒​d𝒗​f​(𝒗)​[B(0)​(ω,q)+B(2)​(ω,q)​v2]=4​π​∫0∞q2​dq​∫0∞d​ω​[ρ(0)​(ω,q)​B(0)​(ω,q)+ρ(2)​(ω,q)​B(2)​(ω,q)],\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \Gamma&=\int{\mathrm{d}}\boldsymbol{q}\,{\mathrm{d}}\boldsymbol{v}\,f(\boldsymbol{v})\,B(\omega,q,v)\\ &=\int{\mathrm{d}}\boldsymbol{q}\,{\mathrm{d}}\boldsymbol{v}\,f(\boldsymbol{v})\,[B^{(0)}(\omega,q)+B^{(2)}(\omega,q)\,v^{2}]\\ &=4\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}q^{2}{\mathrm{d}}q\int_{0}^{\infty}{\mathrm{d}}\omega\,\left[\rho^{(0)}(\omega,q)\,B^{(0)}(\omega,q)+\rho^{(2)}(\omega,q)\,B^{(2)}(\omega,q)\right]\,,\end{aligned} (112)

where ρ(2)\rho^{(2)} is defined analogously to ρ(0)\rho^{(0)}, but with an additional v2v^{2} factor:

ρ(2)​(ω,q)=πq​∫vq∞v3​𝑑v​∫−11d​cos⁡α​f​(𝒗).\displaystyle\rho^{(2)}(\omega,q)=\frac{\pi}{q}\int_{v_{q}}^{\infty}v^{3}\,{\mathrm{d}}v\int_{-1}^{1}{\mathrm{d}}\cos\alpha\,f(\boldsymbol{v})\,. (113)

Appendix D On the isotropy and T→0T\to 0 assumptions

D.1 Isotropy of the material

Following [16], in our derivation we assume isotropy of the detector material. This assumption allows us to:

  • •

    integrate out most of the angular variables in Appendix B,

  • •

    neglect the screening corrections to the transverse responses [16].

Although the assumption of isotropy is not always strictly satisfied, it is often satisfied approximately, to the extent that allows us to neglect the local-field [15] and the screening [18] corrections.

For isotropic and non-spin-polarized materials, the results provided in this work are exact. As we point out above Eq. 27, below Eq. 46, and above Eq. 94, the assumption of isotropy is mathematically equivalent to averaging over detector’s orientation. Thus, for non-isotropic materials, the results correspond to an expected value given the detector’s orientation is chosen randomly, or to a situation in which the orientation changes cyclically (e.g., the detector is rotating). This standard approach has been also used and extensively discussed in, e.g., [21, 13, 18].

D.2 Temperature dependence of the results

In our results, the thermal corrections are encoded in the exponential term e−β​ωe^{-\beta\omega} in Eq. 40. The detectors of interest are assumed to operate in temperatures not exceeding the room temperature, equivalent to ca. 0.025​eV0.025~\text{eV}. This value is very small in comparison to the smallest energies considered in our manuscript, e.g., the one-electron ionization threshold of germanium is 0.67​eV0.67~\text{eV}. Hence, the exponential term in Eq. 40 is completely negligible in comparison with 1, which justifies using the limit T→0T\to 0.

For metals, not considered in our manuscript, those effects could be of some relevance because of the absence of the band gap whose energy would have to be exceeded to induce a signal. For instance, for energy transfer equal to 1​meV1~\text{meV} , the value of the (1−e−β​ω)(1-e^{-\beta\omega}) term in Eq. 40 becomes 0.04≪10.04\ll 1. Nevertheless, to obtain the total interaction rate we integrate over the whole range of allowed ω\omega’s, so that the higher values, with negligible thermal term, should dominate the result and the thermal correction should not significantly affect the ratio between the actual interaction rate and the theoretical optimum.

One should definitely take into account the thermal effects described by the e−β​ωe^{-\beta\omega} term when considering phononic detection channel, for which even the smallest energies may be relevant and could provide a measurable signal. This case is, however, beyond the scope of this work.
